courses.title: The 13th Grade
courses.description: Working on your mindset, your money, and dealing with life's big calls. 24 bite-size units, each paired with a chapter of the book.

units.title: Mindset Hacks
units.blurb: Habits, discipline, and talking to yourself like a coach instead of a critic.
units.action: Tonight, pick one habit, shrink it to a two-minute version, and anchor it to something you already do every day ("after dinner, I open the notebook"). Then write down the emergency version, the one-line move you'll make on the day everything falls apart.
asks: According to the unit, where does the critic voice actually come from?
You blew a presentation. Which line passes the coach test?
Which of these is a standard rather than a verdict?
Why do tiny habits work, according to the unit?
You planned to review flashcards nightly and missed Tuesday completely. What matters most now?
What should the 66-day figure change about how you plan a new habit?

units.title: The Comparison Trap
units.blurb: Instagram is not a benchmark. Building your own scoreboard.
units.action: Go through your follow list once tonight: mute every account that only ranks you, follow two people two steps ahead whose method you can actually see, and write your first three-line scoreboard of what moved this week that you control.
asks: What does a feed do to the brain's comparison machinery that a small town never did?
Why does "delete the apps" fail as a fix within about a week?
Which of these comparisons can actually teach you something?
Why do so many people quit new skills around week three?
What makes "you six months ago" the right opponent?
Why does "just be grateful" fail even faster than deleting the apps?

units.title: First Principles Thinking
units.blurb: Strip a problem down to what's actually true, then rebuild from there.
units.action: Pick one bill or rule you have described the same way for a year. Write it as one sentence, sort its parts into fact, assumption, and custom, and run the single cheapest test tonight: one search, one call, or one email.
asks: In this unit's terms, which of these is a fact?
Why does the teardown test the cheapest assumption first?
Your kitchen-table teardown of a medical question disagrees with your doctor. The likeliest explanation is:
You sign the renewal at $80 more without looking at listings. What did you actually price the increase against?
Dana sells her car, and by week two she has a writeup for a missed shift. What did she get wrong?
Which of these most deserves a teardown tonight?

units.title: Habit Loops
units.blurb: Cue, routine, reward: wiring the boring stuff to run on autopilot.
units.action: Pick one automatic behavior that costs you something. Write its four parts on paper: the cue, the craving (the change of state you want), the response, and the honest reward. Then design one swap that pays the same reward, and make one environment edit that adds twenty seconds to the old response.
asks: According to this unit, the four parts of a habit loop are:
You reach for your phone during a hard paragraph. What does the unit say you are actually craving?
Why does the unit say you rarely delete a loop outright?
Where is the most expensive place to fight a loop, and why?
Dana swaps her bad-day delivery order for cooking a healthy dinner, and the swap dies in four days. What went wrong?
You have quit the same habit six times and relapsed six times. The unit's reading of that record:

units.title: Emotional Intelligence 101
units.blurb: Reading the room, naming the feeling, responding instead of reacting.
units.action: Tonight, find the last message that got a rise out of you. In your notes app, finish two sentences: "I felt ___ because ___" and "It was actually about ___." Then write the reply you wanted to send and save it unsent until morning. Ten minutes, and you have run the whole procedure once at zero stakes.
asks: Why does precisely naming a feeling count as the intervention itself?
"I'm annoyed" versus "I'm embarrassed I did not know that in front of my manager." The difference that matters:
Your heart rate is up and you are mid-draft on a heated reply. The unit's move:
Emotional intelligence keeps getting misread as agreeableness. The actual difference:
A coworker presents your analysis as his own in front of the team, and your anger is accurate. What do you do with it?
Your manager answers your careful plan with "Sure, if you think so." The skilled read:

units.title: Boundaries
units.blurb: Saying no without burning bridges: at work, at home, in the group chat.
units.action: Pick the standing yes you resent most. Tonight, write the boundary as a sentence about what you will do, under fifteen words, zero reasons attached, and say it out loud until it sounds bored. Deliver it this week, and expect the second ask.
asks: By this unit's definition, which of these is actually a boundary?
Why should the boundary sentence stay short?
A week after you set the line, they ask again. The move is:
What usually happens to someone who goes from no boundaries to a fortress overnight?
Your line would be "no messages after seven," but your manager expects answers and you need this job. The honest move:
What actually enforces a boundary?

units.title: Rejection Practice
units.blurb: Getting told no on purpose until it stops being scary.
units.action: Make one real ask tonight that you expect to lose: a fee waiver, a discount, fifteen minutes of somebody's advice. When the answer comes, ask what would have made it a yes, and write the reason down.
asks: Sam makes 5 asks a year and lands 20 percent of them. Dana makes 40 and lands 15 percent. Who comes out ahead?
Why is a cold-email no from a stranger not a verdict on your worth?
Which of these is a real practice ask rather than a stunt?
You just got a no. The most valuable next sentence is:
Six months pass without a single rejection. What does that most likely mean?
Why do second asks, made months after a no, land as often as they do?

units.title: Purpose, Roughly
units.blurb: You don't need a calling. You need a direction and a next step.
units.action: Pick one direction you have wondered about, design its smallest real test with an end date and a yes defined in advance, then send the first message tonight: ask one person who does the work for twenty minutes, coffee on you.
asks: Dana spends forty sincere minutes on the passion page and gets nothing. Why does the page stay blank?
The trap in this unit is hearing its argument as saying what?
Why does a rough heading beat both the detailed ten-year plan and the shrug?
What makes a test "real" by this unit's standard?
Marcus quit the $400 coding course in week five. What did that test actually return?
The interval sentence, "I'm testing a direction right now, and I'll know more by March," works because it does what?

units.title: Money 101
units.blurb: Budgeting that doesn't feel like punishment. Where your paycheck actually goes.
units.action: Find your real monthly take-home from your last two pay stubs or deposits, then schedule one automatic transfer to savings for the morning after payday. Even $25 counts; the pipe matters more than the amount.
asks: The deposit from a $52,000 salary comes in smaller than the math you did on the offer letter. Where did the difference go?
Federal income tax withholding on your pay stub is best understood as what?
You want to get serious about money, so you download an app and log every purchase. Nine days in, you quit. What actually went wrong?
Your needs come to 80 percent of take-home no matter how you trim. What is the honest read?
Why does an automatic transfer on payday beat deciding to save at the end of each month?
In an expensive city your needs land at 62 percent of take-home. Under this unit's rules, what happens to the split?

units.title: Tax Season, Decoded
units.blurb: W-2? 1099? Refund? Plain English, before April ruins your month.
units.action: Pull up your most recent pay stub and find the federal withholding line, so you know what is already being paid in your name. If you have any 1099 income this year, open a separate savings account tonight and move 25 to 30 percent of every payment received so far into it.
asks: Your manager offers a raise from $49,000 to $53,000. A coworker warns it will "put you in a higher bracket." What actually happens?
A $2,400 refund hits your account in April. What does that number actually tell you?
Your first freelance payment lands: $2,000, the full invoice. Why is treating it as $2,000 of spending money a mistake?
Using the unit's invented 20 percent band: which is worth more, a $1,000 deduction or a $1,000 credit?
April 15 is a week away, you owe $1,700, and you have $300. What is the move?
Sasha earned $5,000 at her W-2 job and $5,000 freelancing. Why does the freelance half produce a bigger tax bill?

units.title: Credit Glow-Up
units.blurb: From "no score" to "approved" without falling for a single trap.
units.action: Tonight, find your card's statement closing date (on the statement, and it is not the due date) and work out your reported utilization. If it is over 30 percent of your limit, schedule a payment a few days before the next close or submit a limit increase request in the app. No card yet? Read the full terms of one secured card. Just read, no application.
asks: A credit score is fundamentally a measure of…
Priya charges $950 of her $1,000 limit every month and always pays in full. Why can her score still suffer?
You get a shiny new card and consider closing the no-fee card you opened at 19. What does closing it actually do?
A friend insists you must carry a small balance month to month so the card "has something to score." The truth is…
Two people finance the same $22,000 car over 60 months, one scoring near 750 and one in the low 600s. Roughly what does the difference cost?
You have no credit history at all. Which first move actually starts the file?

units.title: Invest, Eventually
units.blurb: 401(k)s and index funds for people with fifty bucks and a dream.
units.action: Tonight, if you have a job with a 401(k): log in and answer two questions in writing, am I collecting the full match, and what expense ratio does my money sit in. No 401(k) yet? Spend the hour reading how to open a Roth IRA at one large brokerage and write down the three steps you would take.
asks: Your job matches 50 cents per dollar on 401(k) contributions up to 6 percent of pay. Why does claiming the full match come before every other money move?
You collect the full match, you have $250 spare each month, and you carry a card balance at 24 percent. Where does the $250 go?
Maya invests $200 a month starting at 22. Jordan invests $400 a month starting at 32. Under the same assumed return, who has more at 65?
A coworker adds you to a group chat that posts trades and screenshots of wins. How does following it relate to what this unit teaches?
Two years into your plan, the market drops 20 percent in a month. What does the plan say to do?
Which situation means investing is the wrong move this month, no matter how good the argument for starting early is?

units.title: Paychecks & Benefits
units.blurb: The 401(k) match, the HSA, the insurance elections: the form nobody explains.
units.action: Tonight, open your most recent paystub and name every line on it; any line you cannot name becomes an email to payroll. Then log into your benefits portal and confirm three things: the full match is claimed, a beneficiary is named, and your enrollment window is on your calendar. No job yet? Run the drill on the sample stub in this unit so your first real one holds no surprises.
asks: Your gross pay is $2,000 per check but $1,412 arrives. On the paystub, the difference is
A $100 pre-tax deduction only shrinks your take-home by about $75 to $80 because
Offer A pays $52,000 with no match and a $220 monthly premium share. Offer B pays $49,000 with a match worth about $2,000, a $600 HSA seed, and a $60 premium share. The better paid job is
Contributing less than the full employer match is best described as
You miss the thirty day benefits window at a new job. Your health coverage election is now
The fastest way to catch a payroll error is

units.title: Debt, Strategically
units.blurb: Student loans, car notes, and the order to pay them down in.
units.action: Make the one-page list tonight: every balance, rate, and minimum, sorted by rate. Find the minimum-payment box on your worst card's latest statement and read it out loud. Then pick avalanche or snowball, honestly, and point this month's spare dollars at the first target.
asks: Your list shows a $3,100 card at 26 percent and an $18,000 student loan at 4 percent. The emergency is…
Why can minimum payments stretch a card balance past a decade?
In this unit's worked comparison, picking snowball over avalanche cost…
Calling your card company to ask for a lower APR is…
A 0 percent balance transfer is a good move when…
The most expensive version of card debt is usually…

units.title: Emergency Funds
units.blurb: Why three months of rent in a boring account beats any hot tip.
units.action: Tonight, list your survival number line by line and name your most likely single emergency with its price. Then open a high yield savings account at a different bank, move $50 into it, and set an automatic transfer for the day after payday.
asks: The strongest case this unit makes for an emergency fund is that it
"Three months of expenses" is measured against
Why is investing the emergency fund a trap, even at low savings rates?
Marcus pulled $400 from the fund for a bachelor party flight. What actually went wrong?
The first milestone on the ladder is
With no fund, a $900 car repair most often becomes

units.title: Negotiation
units.blurb: Asking for more (salary, rent, bills) without your voice shaking.
units.action: Find one number in your life that arrived looking like a fact: a renewal letter, a recurring bill, a scope that grew. Tonight, write your walk-away number and one comparable, then send the matching one-sentence opener from this unit's table.
asks: Why does the "negotiation as a duel" picture fail for most of real life?
The point of writing down a walk-away number before the conversation is...
They ask for your number first and you know the market. You should...
You said "$1,450" and five seconds of silence followed. What now?
The realistic worst case of a polite, reasoned ask is...
A client keeps adding "small" requests to a fixed-price project. The move is...

units.title: The Big Calls
units.blurb: Career moves, new cities, big relationships: how to actually think them through.
units.action: Tonight, list the three decisions currently circling you and sort each one: two-way or one-way door. Give every two-way door a decision date this week, and for the biggest call, write the question, what would have to be true for each option, and today's date at the top of the page.
asks: A friend has spent a month deciding between two entry-level offers she could quit at any time. The frame says...
Why do people agonize over reversible calls and drift into irreversible ones?
The unit's way to find out how one-way a door really is:
Why write down your reasoning on the day you decide?
You catch yourself calling a lease renewal "basically permanent" and putting the decision off again. What is happening?
What is the daily tax of an unmade decision?

units.title: First Apartments
units.blurb: Leases, deposits, roommates: what to read before you sign.
units.action: Tonight, pick one real listing where you would actually live and finish its math: build the true monthly receipt and the day-one cash pile, then set both against your take-home minus your bills. Keep the two numbers. They are your ceiling for every apartment after this one.
asks: A listing says $1,400 a month. What is the best estimate of what living there costs you monthly?
About how much cash should you have before you start applying for a $1,400 apartment?
Your aunt agrees to co-sign your lease. What did she just take on?
What is the trap inside "spend 30 percent of your income on housing"?
When is your security deposit mostly won or lost?
You paid a $200 holding fee, then the math shows the place is too expensive. The $200 says sign anyway. What is that?

units.title: Career Moves
units.blurb: When to stay, when to jump, and how to tell the difference.
units.action: Spend forty five minutes tonight reading listings for your title and the one above it. Write down the posted pay range and the three skills that keep repeating, then note the last time your resume gained a line that was a result instead of a date.
asks: Why do people who stay in one seat for a decade fall behind their own juniors?
Two offers: $61,000 doing repetitive work alone, or $57,000 with a strong team and real problems. You carry $6,000 in card debt at 24 percent. The move is to...
You ask what the last person in this role is doing now. Which answer should worry you most?
Your company offers you the title Senior Analyst: same pay, same work, plus a weekly leadership meeting. The honest read is...
The case against leaving every job at month eleven is that you keep missing...
You resign, your manager takes it badly, and two awkward weeks remain. The professional move is to...

units.title: New Cities
units.blurb: Moving somewhere you know nobody: the checklist and the math.
units.action: Pick one city you have wondered about and run the leftover math tonight: three real rent listings, a take-home pay calculator set to that state, your transport cost there, and one honest number for the move itself. Even if you never go, the daydream gets a price tag.
asks: Tessa is offered $83,000 in New York against her $64,000 in Columbus. The comparison that says whether it is a raise:
Marcus budgeted $3,500 for his move and it cost $6,900. The gap mostly came from:
The runway rule for landing in a new city:
Month four in a new city feels like proof the move was a mistake. The honest read:
The better use of a lonely new-city weekend:
The clearest sign a move is an escape rather than a destination:

units.title: Big Relationships
units.blurb: Money talks, moving in, and the conversations that decide everything.
units.action: Tonight, alone, write your own answers to the five direction questions: marriage, kids and roughly when, whose career leads, what money you would merge, and what your families get from you. If you are seeing someone, also name the next threshold coming toward the two of you and the date it arrives, because that date is your deadline for the conversation.
asks: What makes sliding so hard to catch while it is happening?
Why can't chemistry resolve a direction conflict?
When is the right time for the direction conversation?
Your answers about kids genuinely do not match. Which move is the dishonest one?
A shared account "just for bills" is best treated as what?
The point of the direction conversation is to do what?

units.title: Health & Insurance
units.blurb: Deductibles, premiums, networks: decoded before you need them.
units.action: Tonight, find the plan you are actually on (yours, a parent's, or the school's) and pull its Summary of Benefits and Coverage from the insurer's site or app. Write down the five numbers: premium, deductible, copay, coinsurance, out-of-pocket maximum. If you cannot find them in twenty minutes, that is the finding; ask HR, the student health office, or the parent whose plan it is tomorrow.
asks: One number tells you the most a covered bad year can cost you. Which one?
You have met none of your $1,500 deductible. A covered urgent care visit runs $400 at the negotiated rate. You most likely pay...
Sam is healthy and could pull $4,000 from savings in a bad month. Priya has monthly appointments and two prescriptions. The honest plan match is...
You schedule a planned surgery at an in-network hospital. The billing question most worth asking beforehand is...
Your job coverage ends June 30 and the new job's plan starts September 1. The move is...
A $2,900 bill arrives six weeks after a covered visit. Your first move is to...

units.title: Family Money Talks
units.blurb: Helping parents, taking help, and keeping all of it healthy.
units.action: Tonight, find the one place money moves between you and family inside a fog: an undated loan, an unspoken expectation, a subsidy with strings. Write down the real numbers, then draft your two sentences, one for the person and one for the request, and put a date on when you'll say them.
asks: Why are family money conversations uniquely hard, according to this unit?
What is the rule for lending money to family or a close friend?
What does separating the request from the relationship let you do?
You built a detailed budget printout to show your mom why you can't keep helping. The unit predicts this fails because...
Why put an amount and a date in writing even on a small family loan?
Your uncle, who has borrowed from half the family, asks you for $400. The unit's move is...

units.title: The Ten-Year View
units.blurb: Zooming out: decisions that compound, and the ones that don't matter.
units.action: Book your yearly review tonight: a recurring calendar event, ninety minutes, on a date you cannot lose, starting within the next month. Then write the first note: one page describing an ordinary Tuesday ten years from now, and one default per domain (money, skill, people, health) that the scene would require.
asks: The unit says nobody can write an accurate ten-year plan. What does it tell you to build instead?
Which of these actually compounds across a decade?
In the ten-year illustration, $200 a month beat four separate $3,000 deposits. What is the real lesson?
You wrote a detailed ten-year plan in January. By March, ordinary Tuesdays keep failing it and you feel worse every week. The unit's diagnosis:
Why does the yearly review insist you write your reasoning down at the time?
Tonight's boring decision, the transfer or the practice session, is hard to make mainly because:

courses.title: The 14th Grade
courses.description: The deeper money course: negotiate what you earn, put it to work, and protect it from taxes, bad products, and scams. 12 units, plain English throughout.

units.title: Salary Negotiation
units.blurb: The script, the silence, and why the first number matters so much.
units.action: Tonight, pull the range for your job title, or the one you want next, from three sources: posted listings in a state that requires ranges, one aggregate site, and one person if you can reach them. Write down your floor and your target, then say the deflection line and the counter line out loud twice each, with your real number in them.
asks: Four minutes into a first phone screen, the recruiter asks for your salary expectations. Why is naming a number now so costly?
An application form will not submit without a salary number. Best move?
Why is negotiating a fresh offer different from asking for a raise a year in?
You named $72,000 and the line has been quiet for five seconds. What is happening, and what do you do?
The recruiter says the base is capped this cycle, and you believe her. The strongest next line is:
You and the manager verbally agree: $66,000 base, a $3,000 signing bonus, a review in six months. What still has to happen today?

units.title: Job Offer Math
units.blurb: Base, bonus, equity, benefits: comparing offers on the full number.

units.title: Side Income
units.blurb: Turning a skill into a second paycheck without burning out.

units.title: Freelance Basics
units.blurb: Contracts, invoices, and getting paid on time, every time.

units.title: Index Funds, Actually Explained
units.blurb: What you own, what it costs, and why fees decide more than skill.
units.action: Tonight, open your 401(k) fund menu or the site of any major brokerage and find one broad index fund. Write down three things on paper: its ticker, its expense ratio, and the expense ratio of the most expensive fund on the same page. That comparison is this whole unit in your own handwriting.
asks: You buy one share of a total market index fund. What do you actually own?
Why can an index fund charge a small fraction of what an actively picked fund charges?
In the unit's illustration, $500 a month for 30 years at an assumed 7 percent growth, what did the extra 1 percent fee cost?
For someone buying monthly and holding for decades, the mutual fund versus ETF question is...
A coworker says index funds are fine for beginners, but real investors pick stocks. The unit's answer?
Your fund falls 30 percent in a bad year. What does the long horizon ask of you?

units.title: The Retirement Alphabet
units.blurb: 401(k), IRA, Roth, HSA: which bucket, in which order, and why.

units.title: Brokerage Basics
units.blurb: Opening an account, placing your first order, and the settings that matter.

units.title: Risk & Time
units.blurb: Why your age changes the answer, and what "risk tolerance" actually means.

units.title: Scam-Proof
units.blurb: The scripts scammers use on smart people, and the two-step habit that beats all of them.
units.action: Tonight, save your bank's real fraud number, from the back of your card, as a contact in your phone, and turn on transaction alerts in the app. Then tell one person in your family the rule out loud: any call about moving money gets a hang up and a callback on a number we already had.
asks: A scam message is most likely to succeed when it reaches you...
Which payment request should end the conversation immediately, every time?
The fraud department calls and your caller ID shows your bank's real name. Why is hanging up and calling the number on your card still the right move?
You deposit a new employer's $2,850 check and your app shows the money as available the next morning. What do you actually know?
Three months into an investment chat with someone you have never met, the platform lets you withdraw $150 of gains, and it arrives. What is that withdrawal?
You realize you wired $800 to a scammer twenty minutes ago. Your first call goes to...

units.title: Taxes, Level Two
units.blurb: Brackets, capital gains, and the moves that legally shrink the bill.

units.title: Insurance, Decoded
units.blurb: What to insure, what to skip, and how deductibles really work.

units.title: Beneficiaries & Wills
units.blurb: The one-page folder your family hopes you have.

courses.title: The 15th Grade
courses.description: Frameworks for the decisions that shape your decade: quitting, moving, buying, marrying, caring for parents. 12 units, no easy answers pretended, real ones worked through.

units.title: Quit or Stay
units.blurb: The four signals that say go, the two that say wait, and the exit done right.
units.action: Tonight, write your stay list: the changes that would make the next year worth having, who controls each one, and whether you have actually asked. Then put a decision date 60 to 90 days out in your calendar before you close the notebook.
asks: You have three years in at a job you now dread. Which way do those three years count in the decision?
Why do people so often stay years past the point a job made sense?
Your job turned miserable the month a new director arrived, and your best stretch here was this spring. The evidence points to...
One line of your stay list reads "my manager stops undermining me in meetings." The method calls that line...
You realize you have left three pursuits in a row somewhere around month eight. What separates a true misfit from the flat middle?
You mostly want out because of the 6 am shift and the ticket queue. Before resigning, the method says...

units.title: Career Pivots
units.blurb: Changing lanes without starting from zero: what transfers and what doesn't.

units.title: Grad School Math
units.blurb: When the degree pays for itself, and when it's an expensive pause button.

units.title: Starting Something
units.blurb: Side project to real business: the checkpoints that tell you to keep going.

units.title: Rent vs Buy
units.blurb: The five-year rule, the hidden costs, and why renting is often the smart move.
units.action: Tonight, run the receipt on one real listing you could imagine buying: an online mortgage calculator for the payment, the listed property tax, an insurance estimate, and one percent of the price divided by twelve for maintenance. Put the total next to your rent, then write down your honest answer to one question: how many years would I stay?
asks: Your uncle says rent is throwing money away. The accurate reply is...
The mortgage payment on a house you like exactly equals your rent. That means...
Why does time in the house matter so much to the rent or buy answer?
Amara saved a $30,000 down payment and calls herself ready to buy. What is she forgetting?
What is the alternative job of a down payment?
The clearest sign someone is buying on the milestone and not the math is...

units.title: Moving Math
units.blurb: New city, new country, new cost of living: the full comparison, not just salary.

units.title: Living With Parents
units.blurb: Moving back home with a plan: saving aggressively without losing momentum.

units.title: First Home Playbook
units.blurb: Down payments, mortgages, inspections: the process from search to keys.

units.title: Partner Money Talks
units.blurb: The five conversations to have before you combine anything.
units.action: Tonight, ask your partner one question: "What did money feel like in your house growing up?" No numbers, no documents, and you answer it too. Single? Write your own answer down in three sentences; it is the half of the conversation you can finish now.
asks: A couple keeps having the same fight about small purchases. What is the fight usually about?
Which conversation does this unit say almost nobody has, and why does it come first?
When does the facts conversation, full disclosure of income, debt, and credit, belong?
What does this unit conclude about the ways couples can structure their money?
Why does opening a money talk with a spreadsheet of your partner's spending backfire?
One partner runs every bill, account, and password. What is the actual danger there?

units.title: Wedding Math
units.blurb: Celebrating big without starting married life in debt, and handling family expectations.

units.title: The Kids Question
units.blurb: The real costs, the real timelines, and deciding on purpose instead of by default.

units.title: Aging Parents
units.blurb: Supporting the people who raised you: money, care, and boundaries that keep love intact.
